İngiltere'de Reform UK Partisi lideri Nigel Farage, Başbakan Andy Burnham'ı İngiltere'yi AB Tek Pazarı'nın bazı bölümlerine yeniden dahil ederek Brexit seçmenlerine ihanet etmekle suçladı. İki tarafın cuma günü Brüksel'de düzenlenen zirvede bir dizi anlaşmaya imza atmaya hazırlandığı sırada konuşan Farage, Brexit tartışmasını yeniden yaşamak zorunda kalmaktan "oldukça öfkeli" olduğunu söyledi.
Burnham'ın temmuz ayında göreve gelmesinden bu yana katıldığı ilk AB zirvesi için Brüksel'e varışı sırasında Euronews'in Europe Today programına konuşan Farage, "Bu sabah Brüksel'de yaşananlar, Andy Burnham'ın bizi gıda ürünleri ve tarım alanlarında yeniden Tek Pazar'a dahil etmesi," dedi.
Farage, İngiltere'nin AB düzenlemelerini kabul etmek zorunda kalacağını ancak bu düzenlemeler üzerinde oy hakkına sahip olmayacağını savundu. Bu adımı, İşçi Partisi'nin Tek Pazar'a yeniden katılmama vaadine ihanet olarak nitelendirdi.
Ancak Farage, Brexit'in İngiltere ekonomisine ve ülkenin uluslararası konumuna zarar verdiği yönündeki Burnham'ın değerlendirmelerine ikna edici bir yanıt vermekte zorlandı.
İngiltere'nin AB'den ayrılmasının ardından küresel etkisinin arttığını savunan Farage, Ukrayna'ya verilen desteği ve Avustralya ile imzalanan AUKUS nükleer denizaltı anlaşmasını örnek gösterdi.
Farage, "Daha güçlü bir konumda olduğumuzdan hiç şüphe yok," dedi.
Brexit'in ekonomik etkilerine ilişkin ise Covid-19 pandemisinin bu sürecin sonuçlarını değerlendirmeyi zorlaştırdığını ileri sürdü. İngiltere'nin yapay zekâ ve finansal hizmetler gibi sektörlerde gelişme kaydettiğini savunan Farage, AB Tek Pazarı'nı ise "başarısızlığa uğramış, gerici bir model" olarak nitelendirdi.
Farage, göç konusunda ise daha açık bir değerlendirmede bulunarak Brexit'in temel vaatlerinden birini yerine getiremediğini kabul etti.
Brexit'in en büyük hayal kırıklığının göçü kontrol altına alamamak olup olmadığı sorusuna Farage, "En büyüğü buydu," yanıtını verdi.
Farage, İngiltere'nin sınırları üzerindeki kontrolü yeniden kazanmasına rağmen rekor düzeyde göçe izin veren politikalar nedeniyle art arda gelen Muhafazakâr hükümetleri suçladı.
Birçok İngilizin Brexit'in vaatlerini yerine getiremediğini düşündüğünü kabul eden Farage, bunun ülkenin AB'ye yeniden katılmasını istedikleri anlamına gelmediğini savundu.
Farage, Burnham'ın AB'ye yeniden katılmayı hedeflemesi durumunda konunun yeniden referanduma götürülmesi gerektiğini söyledi.
"İşçi Partisi, Burnham, bir sonraki seçime AB'ye yeniden katılma vaadiyle girerse referandum yapılması gerekir," dedi.
Alman Sosyalist AP milletvekili Tobias Cremer ise Europe Today programına yaptığı açıklamada Brexit'in İngiltere'ye büyük ekonomik maliyetler yüklediğini ve bugün seçmenlerin çoğunluğunun AB'ye yeniden katılmayı desteklediğini savundu.
Cremer, "Yıllık 260 milyar sterlin, hane başına 10 bin sterlinlik bir maliyet söz konusu. Göç konusunda da durum böyle. Evet, AB'den gelen göç 100 bin ila 150 bin kişi azaldı ancak AB dışından gelen göç aynı dönemde 3 milyon arttı," dedi.
Cremer, 2016'dan bu yana jeopolitik dengelerin önemli ölçüde değiştiğine dikkat çekerek Rusya'nın Ukrayna'daki savaşını, Çin'in artan iddialı tutumunu ve ABD'nin giderek daha öngörülemez hale gelmesini örnek gösterdi.
"Birlikte hareket etmek hem İngiltere'nin hem de Avrupa'nın çıkarına," diyen Cremer, güvenlik, savunma ve ticaret alanlarında daha yakın işbirliğinin her iki tarafa da fayda sağlayacağını belirtti.
İngiltere'nin beş yıl içinde yeniden AB'ye katılmasının mümkün olup olmadığı sorulan Cremer, "Benim de dileğim bu yönde" yanıtını verdi.

İngiltere Başbakanı Andy Burnham, AB Komisyonu Başkanı Ursula von der Leyen ve AB Konseyi Başkanı Antonio Costa, Brüksel'de düzenlenen AB-İngiltere Zirvesi'nin ardından ortak basın toplantısı düzenledi.
Burnham, Brexit referandumunun üzerinden 10 yıl geçtiğini hatırlatarak, "Bugün İngiltere için iyi bir gün, Avrupa için de iyi bir gün. Birlikte vardığımız anlaşma her iki tarafın da yararına ve İngiltere'deki kamuoyunun beklentileriyle uyumlu." diye konuştu.
İngiltere'de halkın dörtte üçünün Avrupa ile daha yakın ilişkileri desteklediğini belirten Burnham, İngiltere Hazinesinin zirvede varılan mutabakatın ülkenin Gayri Safi Yurt İçi Hasılasına (GSYH) yüzde 0,5'e kadar katkı sağlayabileceğini hesapladığını anlattı.
Burnham, yapılan anlaşmalarla İngiliz ekonomisine 17 milyar sterlinlik katkı sağlanacağını söyledi.
Yeni düzenlemelerin işletmelerin bürokrasi maliyetlerini azaltacağını ve gıda fiyatları üzerindeki baskıyı hafifleteceğini ifade eden Burnham, zirvede varılan mutabakatı uygulamaya yönelik yasa tasarısının gelecek hafta İngiltere Parlamentosuna sunulacağını anlattı.
Burnham, anlaşma kapsamındaki çeşitli politika alanlarında yapılacak değişikliklerin uygulamaya konulması için kesin tarihler belirlendiğine işaret ederek, "Eğitim ücretleri gibi çeşitli konularda ilerleyen dönemlerde ayrıca görüşmeler yapılacak. Bu İngiltere için iyi bir anlaşma. Anlaşma, ekonomimize ek bir büyüme, İngiliz halkı için yaşam maliyetlerini düşürme, işletmelerimizin üzerindeki bürokratik engelleri kaldırma ve gençlerimizin ufkunu genişletme fırsatı sunuyor." diye konuştu.
AB Komisyonu Başkanı von der Leyen de tarım ve gıda ürünleri anlaşmasının müzakerelerinin tamamlanmasının büyük bir başarı olduğunu belirterek, "Bu, Manş Denizi'nin iki yakasındaki işletmelerimiz için daha kolay ticaret ve daha düşük maliyet, tüketicilerimiz için daha fazla seçenek ve daha uygun fiyatlı gıda anlamına geliyor." değerlendirmesinde bulundu.
Karbon piyasalarını birbirine bağlayacak anlaşmanın emisyonları azaltacağını ve daha temiz sanayiye yatırımı teşvik edeceğini belirten von der Leyen, İngiltere'nin AB elektrik piyasasına katılımına yönelik çalışmaların sürdüğünü kaydetti.
Von der Leyen, İngiltere'nin 2027'de yeniden Erasmus+ eğitim programına katılacağını, müzakereleri tamamlanan gençlik programının her iki taraftan 100'er bin gence karşı tarafta 3 yıla kadar çalışma, eğitim görme, gönüllülük yapma veya seyahat etme imkanı sağlayacağını anlattı.
Von der Leyen, tarafların kritik teknolojileri ve tedarik zincirlerini korumak için ekonomik güvenlik diyaloğu kuracağını, yapay zeka ve kuantum teknolojileri gibi alanlarda dijital ortaklık başlatacağını, Manş Denizi'ndeki tehlikeli geçişleri önlemek ve göçmen kaçakçılığıyla mücadele etmek için de göç diyaloğu oluşturacağını söyledi.
Pek çok kişinin sonuçlandıramayacağını düşündüğü üç önemli anlaşmaya vardıklarını vurgulayan von der Leyen, "Bunlar, gıda ticareti, gençlerin hareketliliği ve karbon piyasasına ilişkin anlaşmalar. Üçü de önemli birer başarı. Öğrenim ücretleri ise ayrı bir konu. Önümüzdeki ay bu konu üzerinde çalışacağız. Daha önce de çözüm bulmayı başardık, bu konuda da bir çözüm bulacağımıza inanıyorum." ifadesini kullandı.
AB Konseyi Başkanı Costa, Ukrayna'ya destek ile Avrupa'nın güvenlik ve savunma ihtiyaçlarının AB-İngiltere ilişkilerinde yeni dönemin başlangıç noktası olduğunu belirtti.
İngiltere'nin AB'nin sivil kriz yönetimi misyonlarına daha düzenli katılımını sağlayacak çerçeve anlaşmanın müzakerelerinin tamamlandığını anlatan Costa, "Adil ve kalıcı bir barış sağlanana kadar Ukrayna'yı siyasi, mali ve askeri olarak desteklemeye devam edeceğiz." diye konuştu.
İngiltere'nin AB ile uzun vadeli ilişkisine dair tartışmaları ilgiyle takip ettiklerini söyleyen Costa, "İngiltere'nin AB ile uzun vadeli ilişkisinin geleceği konusunda alacağı her karara saygı duyacağız." ifadesini kullandı.
Costa, AB'nin İngiltere ile mümkün olan en yakın ilişkiye açık olduğunu belirterek, tek pazarın dört serbestisinin bölünmezliği ile hak ve yükümlülükler arasındaki dengenin bu ilişkiye yön vermeye devam edeceğini kaydetti.
Zirvenin ardından yayımlanan ortak bildiride, tarafların tarım ve gıda ürünlerinin ticaretini kolaylaştıracak anlaşmayı 1 Mart 2028'den, emisyon ticaret sistemlerini birbirine bağlayacak anlaşmayı ise 2028'den itibaren uygulamayı hedeflediği kaydedildi.
Gençlik programının sunduğu imkanların en geç Ocak 2030'da gençlerin kullanımına açılmasının amaçlandığına işaret edilen bildiride, AB ve İngiltere'nin üniversitelerinde eğitim gören öğrencilerin ödeyeceği öğrenim ücretlerine ilişkin müzakereleri zirveden sonraki 6 ay içinde tamamlamayı taahhüt ettiği belirtildi.
Bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB elektrik piyasasına katılımına yönelik müzakerelerin tarafların nihai mutabakata varması koşuluyla 2027'de sonuçlandırılması hedeflendiği, tarafların çelik ve elektrikli araç tedarik zincirlerini güçlendirmek için birlikte çalışacakları ifade edildi.
AB ile İngiltere'nin savunma kapasitesinin geliştirilmesi, askeri hareketlilik, kriz yönetimi ve deniz güvenliği alanlarında işbirliğini artıracağı belirtilen ortak bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB'nin Ortak Güvenlik ve Savunma Politikası kapsamındaki sivil misyonlarına katılımını sağlayacak çerçeve anlaşmaya ilişkin müzakerelerin tamamlandığı bildirildi.
Bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB'nin Daimi Yapılandırılmış İşbirliği (PESCO) kapsamındaki Askeri Hareketlilik ve Lojistik Merkezleri Ağı projelerine katılımına yönelik çalışmaların ilerletileceği kaydedildi.
AB ile İngiltere'nin Rusya'nın "gölge filosu" ile mücadelede bilgi paylaşımını artıracağı kaydedilen bildiride, yaptırımların delinmesini önlemek ve kritik deniz altyapısını korumak amacıyla işbirliğini güçlendireceği ifade edildi.
Ortak bildiride, Ukrayna'nın bağımsızlığı, egemenliği ve toprak bütünlüğüne desteğin yinelendiği belirtilerek, Rusya'ya saldırılarını derhal durdurması ve tam, koşulsuz ateşkesi kabul etmesi çağrısında bulunuldu.
Ukrayna'nın katılımı olmadan bu ülkede barışa ilişkin karar alınamayacağı vurgulanan bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin Rusya'ya yönelik yaptırımlarda eşgüdümü artıracağı ve Ukrayna'ya güvenilir güvenlik garantileri sağlanması için çalışacağı bildirildi.
Bildiride, AB'nin Ukrayna Askeri Yardım Misyonu ile İngiltere'nin Ukrayna askerlerinin eğitimine yönelik işbirliğini sürdüreceği ve İngiltere, Fransa ile Almanya'nın öncülük ettiği Gönüllüler Koalisyonu ile yakın koordinasyon içinde hareket edileceği kaydedildi.
Ortak bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin siber saldırılar, hibrit tehditler ve yabancı kaynaklı bilgi manipülasyonuyla mücadelede işbirliğini derinleştireceği belirtildi.
Tehditlere ilişkin bilgi paylaşımının artırılması, ortak tatbikatlarla hazırlık kapasitesinin geliştirilmesi ve saldırılara koordineli yanıt verilmesinin hedeflendiği ifade edilen bildiride ayrıca, tarafların demokratik kurumların dayanıklılığını güçlendirmek, seçimlerin bütünlüğünü korumak ve yabancı müdahalelerle mücadele etmek amacıyla yeni bir diyalog mekanizması geliştireceği kaydedildi.
Ortak bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin özellikle Manş Denizi üzerinden gerçekleşen düzensiz göçü önlemek ve göçmen kaçakçılığı şebekeleriyle mücadele etmek için işbirliğini artıracağı belirtildi.
Avrupa Komisyonunun 16 Haziran 2026'da kabul ettiği Manş Denizi Eylem Planı kapsamında ortak faaliyetler yürütülmesi, sınır yönetiminin güçlendirilmesi ve ilgili kurumlar arasında bilgi paylaşımının artırılmasının kararlaştırıldığı aktarılan bildiride, tarafların düzensiz göç, üçüncü ülkelere geri dönüşler, sınır güvenliği ve yasal göç yolları konularını ele almak üzere yapılandırılmış diyalog mekanizması kuracağı bildirildi.

texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.
China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.
In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.
“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.
“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.
Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.
In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.
The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”
Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”
Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”
In an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army said that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”
The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.
In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”
According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.
The Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.
Modeling released Wednesday —based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.
During the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.
The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the plans, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.
In its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.
Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.
Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”
Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the plan.
“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media .
On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay , environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the plan “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting plans until it can review the case.
Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:
The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

Brexit sonrasındaki ikinci zirvede Brüksel'de bir araya gelen AB ve İngiltere, ticaret ve gençlerin hareketliliğini kolaylaştıracak adımlarda anlaştı. Üniversite harçları ise hâlâ pürüz olmaya devam ediyor.
Avrupa Birliği (AB) ve İngiltere, Brexit'ten on yıl sonra yeniden yakınlaşmayı hedefliyor.
İngiltere Başbakanı Andy Burnham , Avrupa Komisyonu Başkanı Ursula von der Leyen ve AB Konseyi Başkanı António Costa bugün Brüksel'de bir araya geldi.
Bugünkü zirve öncesinde, AB ile İngiltere arasında gıda ticareti, iklim politikaları ve gençlerin hareket serbestliği alanlarında iş birliğini artırmayı öngören anlaşmalar üzerinde uzlaşma sağlandı.
Brüksel ve Londra arasında varılan uzlaşma, İngiltere ve AB üyesi ülkelerden gençlerin mevcut vize yükümlülükleri olmadan eğitim görmek veya çalışmak amacıyla karşılıklı olarak seyahat edebilmesini öngörüyor.
Ayrıca çok sayıda hayvansal ve bitkisel ürünün ticaretinde gerekli olan bazı denetimlerin ve bürokratik işlemlerin kaldırılmasında uzlaşma sağlandı. İklim politikası alanında ise AB ile İngiltere'nin emisyon ticaret sistemlerinin birbirine bağlanması planlanıyor. Bunun sanayi ve ticaret sektörlerine de fayda sağlaması bekleniyor.
Üniversite harçları ise taraflar arasında pürüz yaratan konuların başında geliyor. Alman Haber Ajansı'na (dpa) konuşan AB diplomatları ve yetkililerine göre, bu anlaşmaların yürürlüğe girmesi, AB vatandaşı öğrencilerin İngiltere üniversitelerinde ödediği öğrenim harçlarının azaltılması konusunda uzlaşma sağlanmasına bağlı.
AB müzakerecileri, İngiltere'de öğrenim gören gençlere daha pahalı olan yabancı öğrenci tarifesi yerine İngilizlere yönelik harç tarifesinin uygulanmasını talep ediyor. Londra ise bu talebe karşı çıkıyor. AP'ye konuşan isminin açıklanmasını istemeyen bir yetkili, müzakerelerin kolay geçmediğini ancak sorunun çözülebileceğine dair iyi niyet gördüklerini ifade etti.
Öte yandan Ukrayna'daki savaş ile jeopolitik gelişmeler, tarafları birbirine yakınlaştıran unsurlar arasında değerlendiriliyor. Zirve aynı zamanda AB ile İngiltere arasında güvenlik ve savunma alanlarında iş birliğini artırmayı ve düzensiz göçün sınırlandırılmasına yönelik çabaları ele alma fırsatı da sunuyor. AB Konseyi Başkanı Costa, zirve öncesinde yaptığı açıklamada, "Güvenliğimiz ve refahımız birbirine sıkı şekilde bağlı. Bu nedenle güçlü bir ortaklık bizim için hayati önem taşıyor" dedi.
İngiltere'nin 2016 yılındaki referandum sonrasında 2020'de AB'den resmen ayrılmasının ardından taraflar ikinci kez bu düzeyde zirvede bir araya geldi.
İngiltere Başbakanı Burnham, bu hafta yaptığı açıklamada zirveyi Brexit 'in yol açtığı on yıllık zararın giderilmesine yönelik bir adım olarak nitelendirdi. "Brexit'te kazandığımızdan fazlasını kaybettik" diyen Burnham, gelecekte AB üyeliği dahil tüm seçeneklerin masada olması gerektiğini ifade etti. Ancak Burnham, bunun yakın bir zamanda gerçekleşmesinin beklenmediğini de sözlerine ekledi.
İngiltere ile AB arasındaki anlaşmaların hayata geçirilebilmesi için Londra'nın da oluşturulmasında söz sahibi olmadığı bazı AB kurallarını kabul etmesi gerekiyor. Brexit yanlıları ise bu anlaşmaların İngiltere'nin bağımsızlığını zedelediğini savunuyor.
Brexit'in en büyük destekçilerinden olan aşırı sağcı Reform UK partisinin lideri Nigel Farage, AB ile yeniden yakınlaşma planları nedeniyle Başbakan Burnham'ı "ihanetle" suçladı. Farage, BBC'ye verdiği röportajda, "Ticaret yapmak ve komşularımızla iyi ilişkiler sürdürmek için herhangi bir siyasi birliğe ihtiyacımız yok" dedi. Brüksel'deki zirveye atıfla "Burnham'ın bugün yaptığı ihanettir" diyen Farage, AB ile yakınlaşmanın "Çok, çok yakında yeniden katılacak mıyız yoksa dışarıda mı kalacağız tartışmasına dönüşmesinin kaçınılmaz olduğunu" savundu.
Brexit sonrasındaki ilk AB-İngiltere zirvesinde taraflar Mayıs 2025'te bir araya gelmiş, İngiltere'nin AB'den ayrılması sonrasında ilişkileri yeniden canlandırmayı amaçlayan yeni bir stratejik ortaklıkta anlaşmıştı.

Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?
Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.
The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”
“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.
Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.
That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.
For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.
But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.
From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.
Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.
Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.
Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”
It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.
The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement .
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.
The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).
The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.
The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.
The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

Bondholders want SpaceX’s valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach.
Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.
The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.
SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.
It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.
The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.
The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.
SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.
The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.
The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.
More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.
Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.
SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.
Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.
The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.
“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.
“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said.

Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.
The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.
“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”
Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g. OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
The most concerning of the findings was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:
Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.
Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.
Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.
As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging, and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:
The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.
This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.
The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.
Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.
The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.
The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay . The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.
Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg . Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court . The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.
Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction .

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.
“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”
Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.
After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.
And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.
Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”
What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.
“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.
Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.
Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.
“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”
The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.
“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”
Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.
Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”
It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.
Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.
“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”

A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.
In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.
In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”
Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.
Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar said. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”
In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.
The researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar said.
To get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.
Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.
Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.
In October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar said, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very quickly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”
The eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar said. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.
All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.
To predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao showed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.
During the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.
“Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this new energy source inside it,” Karambelkar said. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very quickly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”
The efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.
In AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he said. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”
The team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar said. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.
Telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar said.

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.
Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.
The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.
Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.
Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech , the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.
For Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.
Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.
NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.
So, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.
“The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech said. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.
“With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech said. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”
Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.
“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech said. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”
The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.
“With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech said. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”
While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.
NASA levied new test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company plans to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.
“One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech said. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.
This year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight plan for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion .
“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech said. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”
The new concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.
“One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech said. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”
The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.
Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.
What’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons , NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.
“We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”
